paper_title: Continuation-Guided LLM Evolution of Program Policies and Goal Compilers in Craftax

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Coding agents can synthesize and optimize code-based policies from simulator feedback, allowing the resulting program to act with zero inference model calls. But for long horizon tasks, two challenges arise: local improvements can hurt final success and switching to a new objective requires another expensive synthesis run. We propose a framework that first develops competence by refining the policy through a feedback cascade, moving from episode returns to hierarchical goals and belief updates which can be scored densely from simulator. In the Craftax game, a partially observed and procedurally generated environment, refinements via episode level feedback stall at <1% final-level arrival, whereas with the feedback cascade the optimized policy reaches the final stage 50% of time (28% final boss defeats). Furthermore, to make this competence reusable towards new goals, we factor the previous controller into an environment interpreter $I$ (models, memory, skills) and a rule program $p_0$, and we show that coding agents can optimize a reusable goal compiler $C_θ$ that maps structured tasks $g$ into new rule programs $p_g$. Across five independent compiler searches trained only on short tasks, the resulting compilers successfully transfer zero-shot to longer tasks without any task-specific tuning nor inference-time LLM calls: continuation-scored feedback and a fixed machine with an editable program together turn a single-task competent policy into a reusable one. Code at: https://github.com/vicgalle/craftax-program-policies

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Language models can produce executable control programs and refine them using simulation feedback (Liang et al. 2023; Chaudhuri et al. 2021). During development, coding agent edits program (with explicit state, rules, and memory); at deployment, this artifact is used as policy, without an LLM call at each action. This is an example of neuro-symbolic division of labor, separating expensive search from cheap and auditable execution. The feedback (i.e., what the model sees between refinements) determines the space of feasible policies (Gallego 2026). In long-horizon tasks, where decision maker coordinates behaviors over tens of thousands of actions, this paradigm raises two related questions: what feedback makes code-based policy search effective, and which artifacts should that search leave behind? Consider Craftax (Matthews et al. 2024), procedurally generated survival game in which an agent has 100,000 actions to gather resources, craft tools and armor, manage physical state, combat enemies, and descend through eight increasingly difficult levels. For an early policy, reaching the last level happens in negligible fraction of episodes and depends on decisions made thousands of steps earlier; and using scalar episode rewards quickly confounds the relevant failure. Decomposing the task into stages or subgoals introduces subtle trap: we shouldnt use subgoals local success as source of value, instead, use the continuation it leaves behind. For instance, an agent exploring the Ice Realm (floor 7) may interrupt exploration to fetch food on the previous level and return, but this strategy helps only if the agent survives the trip with enough health and time left to finish the rest of the journey. In the experiments, we observe that across coding agents code updates, an edits effect on reaching the next level vs the same edits effect on reaching the final level are negatively correlated. Hence, the useful statistic to accept policy code update need not coincide with subgoals completion condition. Our framework operates in two stages. Firstly, it proposes feedback cascade so coding agent can progressively optimize code-based policy towards the objective. Over test set of 2048 game worlds, gross episode-level feedback stalled at 0.29% final floor arrivals, whereas the cascade pushed the arrival rate to 50.49%. Further control experiments confirm that coding agents benefit from the proposed harness. Secondly, an already optimized policy creates an opportunity after refinement: its world models, spatial memory and skills encode useful domain knowledge, but this is interleaved with procedural information specialized to the original objective. Our second stage makes that boundary explicit and turns single-task policy into reusable target for code generation of new policies for alternative objectives. Figure 1 depicts the framework. Our paper makes three contributions: (i) framework for coding agents evolving code-based policies that are exposed to cascade of progressively structured feedback, (ii) policy optimization study with strict cohort evaluation and an audit of misleading local feedback, (iii) compiler search experiment testing transfer to unseen task compositions, including longer sequences, without model calls at inference. sections.title: 2 Framework
sections.content: The framework has two stages: improve policy using structured execution feedback towards pre-declared objective, then turn its knowledge into compiler that produces new programs for alternative objectives. We first define the policy and goal interfaces used by both stages.

sections.title: 2.1 Policies and Goals
sections.content: Craftax Full1 has nine floors, from the overworld (0) to the Graveyard (8), where the final boss (Necromancer) is to be defeated. Using RL terminology, at every step the observation is local symbolic map with items, creatures, inventory and intrinsics. To play competently at the game, the agent has to learn its own inner maps of visited floors, ladder locations and resource state. The policy never receives hidden state from the engine at execution. Coding agents can read simulator source code during development (so they are aware of the rules of the game), and can restore complete simulator snapshots to restart an agent from particular state. The policy is program, rather than neural policy trained by gradient descent. Let Xt be the hidden game state, Ot the public observation and Zt the policys persistent memory. At every step t, the policy produces an action At and memory update, potentially controlled by an active internal goal ut: At = πut(Zt), Zt+1 = (Zt, At, Ot+1). (1) Zt includes the current observation and goal context. The policy can have components modeling aspects from the game, i.e. computing beliefs ˆyt = m(Zt) about true but unobserved 1We use the language version of the environment available at https://github.com/Infatoshi/craftax.cu. quantities yt = ϕ(Xt) such as incoming damage, enemy cooldowns or resource depletion. For an external objective g, lets write Jg(P ) = E[Yg(P )], where Yg is binary terminal success indicator. Long tasks often pass through ordered milestones 0, . . . , K, where milestone + 1 can only be reached after milestone k. If Ek denotes reaching milestone within the horizon, with E0 certain, then the objective = reach milestone can be factorized as Jg(P ) = Pr (EK) = K1 (cid:89) k=0 (Ek+1 Ek). Pr (2) In Craftax the milestones are the floors (levels) with = 8 and the horizon is 100,000 steps. Making this factorization explicit helps in locating bottlenecks. For instance, upstream changes alter downstream equipment, health, memory and time, while recovery trips create recurring behavior across floors. Internal and external goals. Because the word "goal" appears in both stages of our workflow, we distinguish internal goals (u) from external ones (g). Internal goals are persistent subroutines inside the policy that organize behavior and code during policy optimization (our stage 1) and inference. They are related to RL options and controlled hierarchical hidden Markov models (Sutton, Precup, and Singh 1999; Murphy 2026), as each internal goal has symbolic entry, completion and abandonment predicates and executes on call stack. For example, parent goal exploring the Ice Realm (floor 7) remains active on the stack while (child) subgoal starts, producing an excursion going back to Fire Realm (floor 6) for resources such as food. At each step, the controller checks if continues, completes or abandons (returning control to parent goal in the later two cases). These invocations define the start and end states for continuation-based feedback. External goals are multi-stage objectives supplied at inference time. For example: reach floor 1, return to floor 0, acquire six coal, and reach floor 2 while maintaining two coal. And this is regardless of which internal goals the policy controller calls along the way.

2.4 Policy Factorization
The optimized policy P ∗ from the previous stage is a mono-
lithic C program, in which general domain competence is
mixed with a strategy that is specialized for reaching the
final milestone (floor 8 in Craftax). In order to reuse that
competence for new objectives, we factor P ∗ into a fixed
domain machine I and an editable rule program p0, which
are both code artifacts (Figure 1b).
sections.content: The machine contains what is needed to survive and act in Craftax: observation processing, persistent spatial memory, world and resource models, navigation and crafting skills, etc. The program p0 says which strategy to follow, and it is written in teleo-reactive rule language (Nilsson 1994). At each step the rules are checked in priority order (survival and combat rules at the top, strategic progression rules below them) until the first rule that matches emits an action. rule can read the public observation, query the beliefs of the machine, update the memory it is allowed to write, and call the skills of the machine. In the other direction, the machine can ask p0 for strategy parameters such as reserve thresholds. Note that neither nor p0 has access to the hidden simulator state. rule program can be interpreted by at run time, or it can be compiled into specialized C++ binary by partial evaluation (Futamura 1999): P0(h) = I(p0)(h), (6) We also require strict empirical parity check. The original policy , the interpreted program I(p0) and the specialized binary t0 must pick the same action at every step, over large set of seeds (Section 3.2). If this holds, the domain dynamics and primitives are kept fixed inside I, while the high-level strategy in p0 is now clean target for code generation, and this is what lets us reuse it for new goals. t0 = mix(I, p0).

Once (I, p0) is fixed, adapting the agent to a new external
task g becomes a problem of code generation. Instead of

(7) As in stage 1, the coding agent optimizes program, but this program now plays the role of compiler instead of specialized policy. This means that θ is executable Python code instead of set of network weights. Given task specification g, fixed translator Encode(g) parses the task into constant stage tables, and the learned emitter Eθ(g) writes the helper definitions for that task and single control rule. The linker Link puts this rule into the base program p0 at fixed priority slot below the inherited survival and safety rules, and it disables the original floor-8 descent controller of p0. Using what already knows, the emitter can adapt resource gathering, safety buffers and floor routing to the task. Task language and verification. In our experiments, task is an ordered sequence = (s1, . . . , sK) of at most eight stages. stage can be navigation milestone reach(ℓ), where the agent has to visit floor ℓ, or resource milestone acquire(v), where it has to hold an inventory stock (and items that it already holds also count). resource stage can also have persistent maintenance constraint maintain(r), with v. The agent has to complete the stages in order and without dying. When stage with maintain(r) is completed, the reserve is added coordinatewise to the active reserves, and these have to be kept until the end of the task. At run time this is enforced with hard action filter, which does not allow spending below the active reserves. To check progress we use an independent monitor that looks directly at the simulator state and does not trust what the controller declares. concrete compilation example. As an example, take held-out task with four stages: reach floor 1, return to the surface (floor 0), acquire six coal while maintaining at least two coal, and then reach floor 2 (Figure 1, bottom; full source in Appendix C.1). From it, the fixed translation Encode(g) builds the target floor array [1, 0, 1, 2] (1 marks the acquisition stage) and the coal stock and hold arrays [0, 0, 6, 0] and [0, 0, 2, 0]. One of our selected emitters looks at this structure and decides that needs preparation for several floors. It then adjusts the equipment buffers and emits clause for upward travel, which the return stage uses. At deployment, all we need to compile new task is to run the frozen Python function Cθ and execute I(pg), without LLM calls and without tuning with rollouts.

sections.content: To compare every stage fairly without selection bias, we froze all 25 checkpoints after optimization and evaluated them on held-out set of 2048 fresh worlds (Appendix D.1). Figure 2 plots final floor arrival and mean episode return against cumulative coding agent output tokens (11.8M tokens total, including reasoning and rejected branches). Main optimization trajectory. Under feedback regime A, mean return rose from 56 to 84 in four rounds and then plateaued there for six more rounds, leaving floor-8 arrival stuck at 0.29%. Switching to structured feedback broke this plateau at each stage: per-floor pass rates (B) lifted floor-8 arrival to 10.45% by round 13, saved-state branching (C) reached 15.09% in round 14, and goal-level refinement (D) jumped to 28.08% in round 15 and 30.18% in round 16. Extending into model and module refinement (E) pushed arrival to 36.23% with the world model and shield, 45.90% with cross-floor modules, and 50.49% after recursive module refinement. Control experiments. Because the main optimization run is sequential, we ran three control experiments to test what happens when certain components of the cascade are removed: 1. Can agents discover floor-level feedback on their own? Restarting from the regime plateau with round 11s agent setup and same token budget, but stating only the final-floor objective. The agent (Ctrl11) independently invented per-floor pass-rate evaluation within 75k tokens, but only achieved 1.46% arrival (vs. 4.74% for round 11 in the main run). 2. Can agents discover cross-floor goal refinement on their own? Restarting from round 14 with round 15s agents and same budget, but omitting our hierarchical goal framework. The Ctrl15 agent kept partitioning work by floors rather than cross-floor goals. It reached 21.78% arrival, falling short of round 15s 28.08%. 3. Can we skip the early cascade and start directly at the goal level? Given the game engine and the full goal-refinement harness from scratch with no initial policy (Scratch), an agent spent 737k tokens (matching round 10 budget) but achieved 0% floor-8 arrival: 31 candidate edits went unpromoted because zero floor-8 arrivals occurred to score continuations. Advanced continuation feedback requires an incumbent that already reaches the endpoint occasionally, which the earlier regimes provide, thus motivating our cascade feedback design. In addition to the common cohort, Table 2 reports held-out frozen comparisons conducted at the end of each major stage on fresh world cohorts, confirming consistent positive gains at every step. Appendix D.2 audits the candidate edits behind these checkpoints, and shows that local measures such as next-floor arrival are poor guide to final-floor gains.

sections.content: Parity check. The port and the extraction rely on the same check. We ran the reference policy once on fixed set of worlds and recorded the action and the skill label that it chose at every decision. candidate was then run on the same worlds from reset, and its action and skill were compared with the recorded ones decision by decision: an episode fails at the first mismatch, or if its length differs. Since the engine is deterministic given the world seed, two policies that agree at every decision go through exactly the same states. There are 64 development worlds (3.2M decisions), which the agents could run themselves, and 256 held-out worlds (12.4M decisions), which they never saw and were only used to confirm the merged result. Port and extraction process. Both steps were carried out by coding agents (Claude Code with claude-opus-5-5), and every change had to pass the parity check (Figure 3). sections.title: 3.3 Goal Generalization
sections.content: Our last experiment tests whether compiler searched on short goal programs can be reused on new programs, including longer ones. Tasks. The tasks were produced by generator which was fixed before running any search: 16 training and 8 validation programs, of 24 stages each, and test suite of 48 programs. The latter has 16 programs for each of the lengths 24, 56 and 78 and, within each length, six are navigation tasks, five are single-resource and five mixed-resource (Figure 4 shows the task language and three of the programs). Floors range over 03 and resources over wood, stone, coal and iron, with programs differing in the order, composition and stock requirements of their stages; none of them had been used during policy development. We only checked syntax and cumulative bounds, i.e. no task was discarded for being unreachable or too hard. Shared compiler search. For the shared compiler we launched five independent searches, each one fresh gpt-6.1-sol context that started from the same starter emitter, diagnostics and allowed training feedback (the prompt is in Appendix E). Each search evaluated exactly three candidate emitters on the 16 training tasks, using 4 worlds per task (192 episodes). The parent run then scored the three candidates on the 8 validation tasks and 8 separate worlds (192 episodes more) to pick one, and this validation feedback was never returned to the coding agent. We evaluated the five selected compilers, not just the best one. No search had access to the test specifications, to the test outcomes, or to the other four searches. Baselines. To separate the effect of the emitted controller from that of the constraints, we used three fixed controls. The first one, Original, is simply p0: it ignores the task, which we score independently. Guards is p0 with the resourcemaintenance constraints, but without goal controller or navigation barrier. Reference adds to Guards prescribed reactive sequence controller (it travels to the active floor, or obtains the tools and gathers the stock). Our method, Shared, uses the emitters selected above. Finally, Per-task tells us what is gained by knowing the task in advance: given the specification of new task, it runs search just for it in the same emitter interface, with fresh coding-agent context, three candidates on 8 tuning worlds and selection on 8 other worlds. We ran Per-task on fixed subset of 12 tasks (for each length stratum, one navigation, one single-resource and two mixed-resource tasks). So Per-task can specialize to its specification and Shared cannot. Progress semantics and hard constraints are the same in all guarded methods. Evaluation. Each method was run on the same 32 fresh test worlds per task (so comparisons are paired across methods), with horizon of 50,000 actions. In total there are 12,672 episodes: 1,536 per fixed control, 7,680 for the five shared searches and 384 for Per-task. Training, selection and test cohorts are disjoint, and both the sources and the analysis were frozen before we saw any feedback from the test worlds. Our primary contrast is the mean success of Shared minus that of Guards. Its interval comes from crossed bootstrap over coding searches, worlds and tasks (Appendix B.2). The other intervals are descriptive and are not adjusted for multiple comparisons. Overall completion. Table 3 has the results on the 48 test tasks. The shared compilers complete 71.30% of them on average, against 36.20% for Guards and 36.91% for Reference. The primary difference is +35.10% percentage points, and Shared needs 13,727 fewer failure-penalized steps than Guards. No guarded method has maintenance violation, while Original has 164. sections.title: 3.4 Costs and Limitations
sections.content: A reusable compiler changes the cost of every future task. After selection, Shared does not need rollout tuning or model calls for new task, although emission and native compilation still take some time. Conceptually, the costs can be written as Bshared(N ) = Bdevelop + (cid:80)N i=1 bcompile(gi) and Bdirect(N ) = (cid:80)N i=1 bsearch(gi), where both are conditional on the common machine and base policy (whose development and factorization also have to be paid for by the whole workflow). In our experiments, each shared search uses 640 logical feedback episodes, or 7.768.36 million steps, and this counts the shared baselines in full for every search. The twelve per-task searches use 960 episodes in total, which is 12.22 million steps. In output tokens, shared search used 13.4k on average and per-task search 7.5k. Each new task thus costs Per-task 80 episodes (about 1.02 million steps) and 7.5k output tokens, and costs Shared nothing. Since Shared is on par with Per-task on the common subset, shared search pays for itself after eight tasks in feedback episodes and after two in output tokens, and the test suite alone has 48. Appendix B.2 has the full accounting. Limitations. First, the lineage is single adaptive development history. The authors introduced each regime when the diagnosis suggested it, so the feedback is confounded with ancestry, though several controls experiments were performed. Second, the synthesized interpreter is Craftax-specific implementation with lot of inherited knowledge, and parity is an empirical check on held-out worlds. Third, goal generalization is restricted to supplied language and one game engine. The composition and progress semantics come from the infrastructure and each per-task baseline is single search.

sections.title: 4 Related Work
sections.content: Programmatic reinforcement learning searches over structured policy spaces (Verma et al. 2018; Trivedi et al. 2021; Liu et al. 2023), and language-model-guided search adds code proposals made by language model (Liu et al. 2025). Code as Policies generates executable control from instructions, Voyager develops reusable skills, and WorldCoder writes executable world models (Liang et al. 2023; Wang et al. 2023; Tang, Key, and Ellis 2024). In our case, the object that is deployed is frozen program-to-program map over supplied goal language, and the language model only takes part in development. FunSearch and AlphaEvolve combine edits written by model with automated evaluation (Romera-Paredes et al. 2024; Novikov et al. 2025). Dense feedback can expose failures that look the same under scalar score (Gallego 2026). Our feedback cascade also changes the starting state of the comparison, the scope of the code and the continuation. Savedstate branching is related to restoring states for exploration (Ecoffet et al. 2021), although here the paired continuations are used to evaluate local program edits against the chosen endpoint. Options and hierarchies of machines formalize temporally extended behavior and partial control programs (Sutton, Precup, and Singh 1999; Parr and Russell 1998). MAXQ distinguishes the recursive optimality of subtask from the performance of the whole hierarchy, and ALisp takes into account what follows subroutine through its exit value (Dietterich 2000; Andre and Russell 2002). Our continuation formulation applies the same distinction to the edits of coding agents and to handoffs between programs. Policy sketches and reward machines also expose task structure for composition (Andreas, Klein, and Levine 2017; Toro Icarte et al. 2022). In our case the task semantics and the monitor are given, and the code search adapts how the controller uses the skills it already has. The resource guards are similar to runtime shields (Alshiekh et al. 2018), but without synthesized guarantee on the winning region. Goal-conditioned reinforcement learning trains single network over goal space, and the generalization comes from universal value function approximators and hindsight relabeling (Schaul et al. 2015; Andrychowicz et al. 2017; Liu, Zhu, and Zhang 2022). In Craftax, Matthews et al. (2026) train neural policies over discrete set of semantic goals by outputting values for all goals at once (LEO). Our goal compiler can be seen as programmatic family of goal-conditioned policies: the goal enters through code generation over fixed machine instead of as network input or output head, the generated program can be inspected and runs without model, and generalization is tested on multi-stage compositions with constraints that are longer than any seen in training.

5 Conclusions
In order to be useful, a program policy first has to acquire
competence and then expose it in a form that new objectives
can reuse. In this work, feedback that becomes progressively
more structured took the policy from a final floor that was
almost never reached to 50.49% arrival. The continuation view
explains why gains in local completion and in local prediction
have to be separated from their downstream value. Factoring
the resulting policy into a machine and a rule program opens
a second search space, the one of goal compilers. The five
frozen compilers that we obtained transfer from short training
programs to longer unseen compositions, without model calls
for the new tasks, and a single compiler search pays for itself
after eight tasks when compared with searching for each task
separately. Overall, our contribution is a connected neuro-
symbolic workflow for developing and reusing executable
control, in which the model searches over programs and the
program acts.

sections.content: B.1 Cohorts, Selection and Researcher Roles Policy development. An episode counts as an arrival when the deepest floor it reaches is at least 8. The native return adds up the achievement and health terms of the evaluator. For the mean achievement coverage we take the arithmetic mean of the fraction of the 67 distinct achievements obtained (note that this is not the weighted aggregate score of the benchmark). The evaluations last 100,000 actions and they continue after arrival, so later boss victory can be recorded too. In this way, arrivals, victories and native return come from the same complete episode, but each of them describes different outcome of it. For the common-cohort evaluation, the command-line seed is 81,000,000, and we use 2,048 episode indices with the archived SplitMix64 seed scheme. This evaluation was only used to place checkpoints chosen beforehand, and its source list was fixed before any outcome was seen. The plan was originally 4,096 worlds. It was reduced to 2,048 for runtime reasons, before any completed chunk had exposed outcomes, and the dated amendment is kept. This cohort is not the same as the development banks, nor as the frozen campaign tests of the selected programs. In rounds 1516 the development comparison used 512 worlds and seed 53,000,000. The entry banks for round 15 were captured from round 14, on 16,384 worlds with seed 52,000,000, while later screening and confirmation used other development streams. One thing to keep in mind is that continuation is not an independent world, because several entries and random replicas can come from the same source world. When regions are merged, we check the candidate of the agent that owns region against the exact integrated source up to the boundary of that region. In the round-15 merge, all 144 pairs that we sampled have the same action hash, length, deepest floor and death. These checks tell us that the code composes correctly under the ownership convention. sections.content: Memory and boundaries. The program keeps its own maps, both local and global, together with the cells it has visited, the ladders it knows about, the resource sites and what it estimates about adversaries. Each internal goal has frame that holds its identity and its local state, but the persistent world memory is shared between parent and child. We use post-observation boundary convention, which means that the runtime advances at most once for each new observation. Note also that completing resource trip is not the same as physically returning: return event gives control back to the caller even if the child has abandoned its resource objective. If the agent dies, all the active invocations are unwound. Finally, when runtime is inserted it must preserve the actions that already existed, and only after that can new behaviors be enabled. The following schematic shows the timing convention. It is only an illustration, and it does not replace the retained implementation: observe_public_state(); update_world_and_resource_memory(); if (dead()) return_all(DIED); else if (active_goal_finished_or_abandoned() ) return_to_parent(recorded_outcome); /* Survival rules retain higher priority. */ execute_first_rule_that_emits_an_action(); The source bridge. Several steps separate the policy of the main lineage from the program that is factored. The arrivalfocused lineage ends at Final. We then refined Final for the boss fight (Appendix D.4) and froze the boss-refined policy as the baseline of the execution-cost study. That study rewrote it in C++ for speed while keeping every autonomous action and skill label unchanged (the parity check checks both), and we factor the C++ version. The extraction into the rule language is the step that exposes the strategy as p0 over I. Then the composition study freezes 35 dependencies between the machine and the program, and it checks the image of the base program. After extraction, the program has 149 ordered rules, 152 helper definitions and 24 query answers, which are spread over seven files. The language supports typed integer and float operations, local arrays, out-parameters and static call frames. When it is deployed, the program calls the primitives of the machine through exported interfaces, and the machine calls back to the program through explicit queries whenever it needs strategy parameter. There is also commanded-goal mode, which still has its own code, but we disable it in the composition study. Port and extraction process. We give here more details on the two steps of Figure 3. In the first part of the port, the two agents owned disjoint parts of the code (the path search, and everything else), and root agent merged their snapshots at checkpoints. The time per decision went from 47.6 to 12.4 µs. Recompiling this code as C++23 ran at exactly the same speed, so in the second part three agents started from the plain port and each one pushed different property: time per decision (1.28 times faster), memory per instance (from 1.33 MB to 349 KB) and compile-time guarantees, where the compiler itself replayed the first 3,400 steps of development episode and checked every action. fourth agent combined the first two, and the result is the target t, with 350 KB per instance. Along the way the agents reported four bugs, none of which changes autonomous play. As for the extraction, in the second stage the root agent first extended the interface in both directions: p0 exposes four entry points (initialization, observation, action filter and commit), and may call p0 back through queries whenever generic routine needs strategic parameter. Each of the three subagents owned one area of the code and had to keep parity on the development worlds at every snapshot, while the root agent merged the snapshots and reran parity, on the held-out worlds as well. The C++ policy has 510 literal floor references. After the first stage 266 of them are in p0 and 259 in I; at the end, p0 has 467 and the decision path of has 24, e.g. which floors are lit or where the boss is. On our side, we only proposed the two questions of the port (the inference cost, and what C++ adds), chose the policy to factor and launched the second stage. Parity and specialization. The dynamic evaluator loads typed image of the nodes. The specialized evaluator does something different: it turns the node indices into template parameters and the node data into constants. Since both of them use the same helper for each operation, the arithmetic and the order of side effects are the same in the two. Both builds of the final factorization (interpreted and specialized) agree with the C++ target on 64 development worlds, with 3,209,631 decisions, and on 256 held-out worlds, with 12,354,934 decisions. To catch cases where the program depends by accident on old contents of the scratch memory, we poison that memory first. The criterion that we use is strict: the action and the skill have to be the same at every tested step, so having the same aggregate reward is not enough. The report also includes timing trace, where we kept the best of three runs in that session. The C++ target needs 9,438 ns per decision, interpretation needs 19,714 and specialization 9,493, which means that specialization gets back the overhead added by interpretation. For the task-conditioned policies we did 28 more comparisons between interpreted and native execution. These match in rows and action hashes over 262,588 decisions, on the training and tuning worlds that were allowed once the source was closed. C.1 Worked Goal-to-Program Example For this example we take test program with four stages, and the emitter that was selected in shared search 5. The reason for choosing it is that it has return, an acquisition and also maintenance bound that applies later on. The displayed source is the program that this emitter generates for the task. One goal becomes policy program Input goal (a held-out task) reach(1); reach(0); acquire(coal 6), maintain(coal 2); reach(2) Fixed translation: stage tables const int sq_floor[]={1,0,-1,2}; Coal columns: stock = [0, 0, 6, 0], hold = [0, 0, 2, 0]. Selected emitter: controller excerpts const SR_SIMPLE=0; if(target<a.level)return travel(0); Figure 7: Translation of concrete task, and the source that the selected emitter produces for it. The coal columns show only part of the full tables, which cover five resources. Milestone semantics belong to the fixed translation, and the controller strategy belongs to the emitter. The parser accepts floors from 0 to 8 and bounds from 0 to 20 for wood, stone, coal, iron and diamond, but the generator in our experiment only uses floors 03 and never asks for diamonds. reach stage is completed when the agent stands on the requested floor, and an acquisition stage when all the named inventory bounds hold. The monitor accepts at most one milestone transition per observation, and only while the agent is alive. Items already in the inventory can count towards later acquisition. Maintenance starts once that acquisition is completed and lasts until the task ends, using the coordinatewise maximum of the bounds completed so far. The task fails if there is violation, if the agent dies, or if the horizon runs out first. Going back to the example, the floor table is [1, 0, 1, 2] (1 is the acquisition stage), the coal stock column is [0, 0, 6, 0] and the hold column is [0, 0, 2, 0]. Once the third milestone is reached, the bound of two coal remains active while the policy goes on to floor 2. Since the goal goes further than floor 1, the emitter in the figure sets SR_SIMPLE=0, and in its branch for difficult goals more of the equipment preparation of the base program is kept. For the returns, it emits clause for upward travel that reuses the navigation already in the machine. Other selected emitters have their own rules for reserves and routing. Audit and monitor boundaries. What the emitter is allowed to see is the structure of the goal and the public interfaces. The search rules forbid few things explicitly: behavior that depends on the name of the goal, access to world seeds or to results, external I/O, replacing the common semantics, and writing into the task-progress fields. We enforce these rules with static checks on the Python and TR code, and we also reviewed the source manually. The monitor reads the native engine state on its own and never trusts the progress that the policy reports, nor the completion predicates that were emitted. The hard filter blocks resource spending that would cross an active positive reserve, but it adds no navigation barrier, and all guarded methods use this same filter.

Inside goal the situation is similar. Round 16 has nineteen candidates with favorable local measure, and not one of them has supported floor-8 gain. One example is lighting excursion: it is completed in one action and it reduces damage over short window, but arrivals go down, both for single invocation and under repeated use. In addition, fifteen candidates with positive one-invocation estimate were also tested repeatedly, and nine of them shrink or change sign there. That is why all accepted modules were selected under repeated use from entry states, scored by the endpoint. Candidate accounting. The ledger has 56 edits from round 15 and 96 from round 16 (152 in total), but only 24 candidates were tested both with single invocation and under repeated use. Nineteen had positive repeated-use screen and went to disjoint confirmation; twelve of them kept their sign and three had intervals above zero. Recall that the ledger records an adaptive search, and thus includes superseded variants and implementation fixes as well. Goal ownership. Inspecting the logs, we noticed that roughly third of the episodes which get to the Ice Realm end with the agent dead in an excursion to an earlier floor. Our response in round 15 was to make the excursions goal of their own, with its own coding agent, alongside the Ice agent and the other regions. On the common cohort, the Ice pass rate then rises from 0.41 to 0.64. Since there was no persistent runtime until round 16, we attribute this gain to the Figure 8: Round-15 modules: effect on arrival at the floor that ends each region (the local proxy) against the effect on floor-8 arrival, in percentage points with 95% intervals. Filled markers are retained modules. (Spearman ρ = 0.71, Figure 8), with single module having supported gain on both. E.g., three variants for floors 34 looked promising as they improve floor-5 arrival by about eight points, but we did not retain them since they have no supported gain on the final floor. Conversely, there is an early-floor variant that reduces floor-3 arrival by 1.85 points while improving floor-8 arrival by 4.33 (both intervals exclude zero). In other words, which edits look useful depends on the decomposition and the ownership. Models and decisions. The world model had specific error, as it did not predict point-blank projectile attacks; we fixed this, and added safety filter that vetoes the actions predicted to be fatal by rollouts based on public observations. These two fixes modify the actions immediately. Their audits therefore compare trajectories that diverge, and acceptance is decided by the endpoint tests. resource model came later. It is inert, in the sense that it only tracks the time until each resource runs out and the cost of trips. We tried planner that reads it on every floor: the awake steps without water were halved (from 71.7 to 37.0) but floor-8 arrival dropped by 2.34 points, the reason being that the planner routes the agent past guarded water. Restricting the planners scope helps. This is case in which better predictions and better local statistic do not give better final decision. Goal and model examples. Take for example kit goal that raises the armor at the entry of the Troll Mines from 4.30 to 4.54 and completes 60% of its calls. Its effect on floor-8 arrival is only +0.01 points, with interval [0.61, 0.64] over 8,516 paired continuations. This happens because plate can replace an iron piece instead of filling an empty slot, and producing it can displace diamond pickaxe. Goals that are placed on trips the policy already makes are more effective: the strategic kit-goal composition increases arrival from 30.91% to 34.06% on 4,096 reserved worlds, which is +3.15 points with interval [1.86, 4.44]. Note that this cohort is different from the one where it is placed at 31.45% in Table 5. In the world-model campaign we found point-blank shots that the model did not predict. After repairing the model, the unpredicted projectile hits go down from 1,778 to 825 on diagnostic bank of 400 continuations. The safety filter runs 24 short rollouts, eight steps each, with model that only uses public beliefs. We measured its effect on the endpoint together with the model repair, as one composition, so the reset gain in Table 2 cannot be attributed to prediction accuracy alone. Later on, module refinement adds an inert resource model, and the editing moves from regions of the episode to modules for navigation, supply, combat and equipment, which span several floors. Because these modules share state, integration tests are still needed. D.3 Recursive Follow-ups We report the outcomes of all five campaigns in Table 6. Under the declared final comparison, only campaign 3 promotes its candidate, and its gain of +3.81 points is relative to the incumbent of the campaign. If we compare it instead with its immediate internal parent, on the same cohort of 1,024 worlds, the final child adds only +0.49 points with interval [2.47, +3.45]. This means that we cannot say how much this last child contributes on its own. D.4 Boss-Victory Extension then arIf the external objective is to win the game, rival becomes subgoal itself. This is useful, because the saved arrivals can then be used for paired continuation comparisons and we do not need to replay the whole approach each time. There were three campaigns, which refine the combat, search and recovery children, and each one freezes candidate before it goes through separate reset test  (Table 7)  . The first candidate extends the safety filter and repairs the finishing attacks. The second one does not pass the promotion rule, so it is not installed. The third one is the one we retain. It adds progress tracking based on public observations: when the search stalls it triggers lighting and repairs the firing line, and in safe windows it lets the agent prepare potions. Then we evaluated on the common cohort of 2,048 worlds. There, the boss policy (selected in advance) wins 581/2,048 episodes (28.37%), compared with 183/2,048 (8.94%) before the boss refinement. In total 453 wins are gained and 55 are lost, which is paired gain of 19.43 points with interval [17.45, 21.42]. The two policies reach floor 8 in exactly the same 1,034 worlds, and for the 1,014 episodes that do not arrive the records are identical. If we condition on arrival, the probability of winning rises from 17.70% to 56.19%. Note that the gain is due to the complete composition, and that this cohort is not the one used in the campaign tests.
